# Zero Punctuation: Hatfall Review — Absurd, Fast, and Surprisingly Addictive

Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition is exactly the kind of game that looks ridiculous at first glance, and then somehow becomes way more fun than expected.

At its core, Hatfall is simple: hats fall, you catch them, chaos happens. That is the pitch, and honestly, the game knows it. It does not try to pretend it is bigger or deeper than it is. Instead, it takes one very silly idea, wraps it in sharp comedy, weird timing, quick reflexes, and Zero Punctuation-style absurdity, then keeps escalating until the whole thing becomes strangely addictive.

The best part of Hatfall is how immediately playable it is. You can understand the basic idea almost instantly, but the game keeps throwing enough nonsense at you to stay entertaining. It is fast, readable, and funny in a way that fits the Zero Punctuation brand perfectly. The jokes, visual style, and general attitude all feel like they belong together.

What makes it work is that the comedy is not just sitting on top of the game. The entire design feels like a joke that became an actual arcade game. It is intentionally stupid, but in a smart way. Every mistake, weird animation, sudden interruption, or ridiculous moment adds to the experience instead of feeling random for no reason.

The game also has that strong “one more try” energy. Runs are quick, failure is easy to laugh at, and improving feels natural. It does not need a massive open world, deep story, or complicated systems. It just needs timing, reaction, comedy, and hats. Somehow, that is enough.

It is not going to be for everyone. If you do not like Zero Punctuation’s humor, the style may not land. If you need a long, serious, feature-heavy game, this probably is not what you are looking for. Hatfall is short, silly, and very specific in tone. But that focus is also why it works.

For stream or video content, this is a great little hidden gem. It is easy for viewers to understand, fast enough to keep momentum, and weird enough to create reactions. The yellow visual style, absurd premise, and comedy timing make it stand out immediately.

My verdict is Hidden Gem.

Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition is a great example of a small comedy game that actually understands how to be fun. It is simple, chaotic, funny, and much more addictive than it looks.

It is not trying to be a masterpiece. It is trying to make you catch hats while everything gets increasingly stupid.

And somehow, that makes it great.

Final Verdict: Hidden Gem

The Hatfall game, created by Yahtzee Croshaw, retains the fundamental idea in its Steam version: players must catch a falling hat while navigating through decoys and hazards, with the challenge escalating as more characters fill the screen. This version introduces countdown mechanics, mini-games, achievements, and cosmetic hats.

-Humor Atmosphere: The game offers humor and variety, featuring Easter eggs that encourage repeated play with its absurd premise and occasional comedic elements. However, it demonstrates minimal involvement from Yahtzee, lacking direct narration or satire, with humor appearing only in sporadic instances.

-Gameplay: While it is easy to learn and remains engaging as the difficulty increases, players must catch hats and avoid hazards. Nevertheless, it suffers from a lack of depth, with limited gameplay variety beyond the hat-catching mechanic, resulting in a grindy experience due to slow progression and minimal rewards.

Zero Punctuation: Hatfall stands out as a brief, quirky time-killer that holds nostalgic value for fans of Yahtzee; however, it does not provide a profound or enduring experience. It is best enjoyed by those who appreciate light distractions and absurdist humor, particularly during sales or as a novelty. I score this game 7 Stones out of 10 rock and stone.

Is this game going to have tonnes of replay value? No. Will it keep you engaged for at least a little while to play through each of the mini-games? Probably. 

It's a fun little concept in the same way that cookie clicker is; a time waster to play when you don't really have the commitment for a proper title. You run left to right in hopes of catching a hat that descends from the heavens. Then the game starts to fight you and makes collecting these hats more of a challenge by adding in extra characters to blur your perception on who it is you're controlling. You, or possibly these additional characters, may be crushed or impaled should anyone happen to misstep and end up in the wrong place.

The wizard will further add to this difficulty by altering reality, either by means of raining down slippery blood, or rotating your screen 180 degrees... Or, at least I think he rotates your screen, I can't be bothered to reinstall and find out. Appease him and he may grant you a boon. 

After you finish collecting a specific amount of hats, you are then able to do one of two things:
Option 1 is to purchase an alter-ego from the store who will appear when clouding your screen. Option 2 is to redeem a gift that is periodically magnetised to the hat you have just caught. These gifts that you redeem are the core basis for keeping you engaged as they're what unlocks the mini-games. 

The mini-games are certainly whimsical, there's a hat dating simulator in full on Japanese style. Then there's the one where you hide in a tree, shoot a bear accountant, then take his place at work. There's also less intense gags like rolling down a hill at your desk to catch hats in a net and It's just dumb fun. If you liked Zero Punctuation and enjoy absurd comical things, then for £5 you may as well take a look.

In conclusion: Where's your hat? You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hatless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

[i]Zero Punctuation: Hatfall: Hatters Gonna Hat Edition[/i] is a comedic score attack game about collecting hats. Created by [i]The Escapist[/i]'s Yahtzee Croshaw, this short game faithfully captures the spirit of Yahtzee's show [i]Zero Punctuation[/i], and thus is sure to please its fans. It boasts a surprisingly deep narrative and upgrade system that promote solid replayability for such a simple concept. While achievement hunters will struggle with the unreasonably high thresholds for the final achievements and all players will face some graphical bugs, there's enough here to justify a purchase for interested players, especially visiting fans.

In [i]Hatfall[/i], you run back and forth to collect hats until you miss one. Levels get progressively harder as the screen clutters with more NPCs and the game throws in other threats and distractions. The hats serve as both a currency to unlock "upgrades" and as a nebulous counter on the main menu until...something happens. The upgrades, while mostly cosmetic, can segue into odd minigames that often involve branching choices such that you'll want to buy them again to see all the options - thus, the replayability.

The game's writing, between the minigames, the quotes on interstitial screens, and everything relating to the countdown exude the comedic energy of [i]Zero Punctuation[/i]. Crass humor, political digs, mockery of videogame tropes, exotic profanity - whether one is a fan of Yahtzee's humor generally would serve as a good litmus test for how well one would enjoy this game's writing. Though some of the jokes can grow stale through the repeats that extended play sessions entail, there is enough writing to satisfy the 3-4 hours it takes to resolve the game's "plot."

As a score attack game, this is the ideal kind of subject for achievement hunter or score attackers. Unfortunately, the most difficult achievements require way too much dedication. As mentioned, there are roughly 3-4 hours of fresh content to explore - and then look at my playtime. These achievement requirements should've been cut in half, at least. To compound the inconvenience, this game has no Steam Cloud support, meaning that all progress for one of the hardest achievements resets everytime the player uninstalls. Otherwise, beyond some non-gamebreaking graphical bugs, there is little to complain about.

[i]Hatfall[/i] feels like a gift specifically tailored for [i]Zero Punctuation[/i] fans. The extremely basic premise and short runtime offer little draw on their own, but the knowledge of being able to enter a playable realm of Yahtzee's making all the while supporting the creator himself and enjoying some otherwise forgotten content should make this a gratifying purchase for fans. And for the non-fans, it can serve as a nice introduction too! [i]Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition[/i] gets a B-.

Welcome to opposite day, where gamers all come together to review a game made by a well known game reviewer! The sun will be cold, pizza is a weight loss food, and I'm considered funny. Everything is topsy-turvy... right up until the end of this paragraph. 

Oh, well that was short lived. Hatfall, then... 
I am torn between my thoughts. On the one hand, it's a simple little mobile game that is squatting on Steam with the big boys. On the other hand, I've sunk over 6 hours of my life into this little mobile game. If I didn't like it, I'd have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ off before even hitting 30 minutes. Am I biased because I just like Zero Punctuation? The answer is almost certainly, nearly, entirely, not-unlikely to maybe be: Yes?

Okay, what is Hatfall? It is a game where you put on hats. That was simple. So, I spent 6 hours trying on hats? "Ooh, the writer at Overlord Arcade must have a lot of free time on his hands." crow the users at Steam. Well, yes and no... you see, it's got depth in the same way a clicker game has depth. Once you've put on a metric ♥♥♥♥-ton of hats, falling from the sky like a haberdasher's airplane exploded mid-delivery, then you enter the 2nd half of the game... which is exactly the same, but now there is a big hat monster in the sky. After that, there's some additional whatnot available, but I'm not feeling spoiler-y, and then, wallop... back to square one you go!

Game play is extremely straight forward. There are X amount of characters on the screen, and you don't know which one you are. Sometimes it's you and an imp, which look completely different. Sometimes it's you and another similar lady/fella, but they look just different enough to stand out. the 3rd type of character looks just like you, and half the time will mimic you movement so damn closely, that you're guess will be a 50/50 as to whether you're following the right chump, as you scan the screen like a coke fiend, looking for ticks and tells. Once you've nailed down who you are, be under the hat when it falls. Simple enough, yeah?

It's simple when there's just hats, but sometimes, you've got to dodge signs, cars, poles, and anvils. Each thin also plummeting down, ensuring that that previously mentioned haberdasher really branched out at some point, obviously using a cargo plane the size of the moon. Even then, sometimes you will call down the wrath of a local wizard, by the mere offense of putting on his magical hat. I kind of figured he would be grateful to not have his big brimmy boy slapped down in the mud, but there you go. Wizard mad, and coin flip on how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are on the next screen. There are about... 3-4 zany modifiers that can apply for these, which run the gamut of being either hardly a nuisance or run-ruiningly cheap. 

I think what will keep players glued are the little gifts you unlock as you go on. No doubt you've seen pics of that big anime eyed trilby, if you've so much as glanced at the store page. After a handful of hats collected, you'll be rewarded with a gift, and these range from cosmetic only, to little bonus mini-games that will show of some of the quirkier bits of content. 

On the whole, do I recommend Hatfall? I think the better question is do you like Zero Punctuation? If the answer is yes, then this is more ZP style and humor. There's a game in here as well, and the game is fun enough. Just remember that it's a mobile game, and you'll be equally as satisfied with that level of expectation. I, for one, really like ZP and enjoyed this game enough to drop about 6 and a half hours on it. I've gotten close to 100%-ing the thing, so take that as a measure of how deep the content will go, I suppose. If you'd like to see exactly what kind of shenanigans I get up to during this long boy, Drop by the YouTube channel and enjoy a brief glimpse into Hatfall.

A simple, heartfelt game about the repeated transfiguration of a non-Yahtzee entity into Yahtzee. What more can be said? It has fast-paced, repetitive gameplay occasionally broken up by little additions or distractions which in and of themselves get old eventually. It has some amusing writing and a fair bit of filler. It makes me smile when I miss a hat and hear Yahtzee going "Wronnngg!", but that also makes me wonder why his voice and intonation -part of the core of Zero Punctuation, arguably more important than the distinctive visuals and nearly as important as the clever writing- would be featured so little in a game wearing the ZP label. Feels like a missed opportunity.

Overall, it's a bit of fun for an hour here and there, but not the best value for money even at a relatively low price point. If you're a big fan of Zero Punctuation... I'd frankly recommend you just watch more of that.

Oh, and if you'd still like to support Yahtzee while also getting a game you can actually get some gameplay out of for your money, check out The Consuming Shadow.
